steps.text:
Welcome, [b]General[/b]. The United Kingdom is yours.

Before we fight, learn to read the table. This will be brief.

First, the [b]map[/b]. Every country you can hold, supply and score is on it.

Pan with [b]W A S D[/b] or the arrow keys. Zoom with the [b]mouse wheel[/b]. Go on, look around.

Six [b]factions[/b] fight this war: [b]Germany[/b], [b]Italy[/b] and [b]Japan[/b]; [b]the United Kingdom[/b], [b]the Soviet Union[/b] and [b]the United States[/b].

Each has its own hand, its own units and its own score.

Those six form two [b]teams[/b].

Germany, Italy and Japan are the [b]Axis[/b].
The UK, the Soviets and the US are the [b]Allies[/b]. That is your side.

You score for yourself, but you win as a team.

The three factions' points are added together into the team totals shown here.

A [b]round[/b] is one turn for each faction, always in this order, top to bottom:

[b]Germany[/b], [b]UK[/b], [b]Japan[/b], [b]Soviet Union[/b], [b]Italy[/b], [b]United States[/b]

Germany moves first, and you answer immediately.

Every turn runs five steps, shown up here:
[b]1. Play[/b] one card, or discard one
[b]2. Supply[/b]: cut-off units are removed
[b]3. Victory[/b]: score your supply stars
[b]4. Discard[/b] cards you do not want
[b]5. Draw[/b] back up to seven

[b]Play[/b] is the heart of it: one card, once, and the turn is spent.

[b]Discard[/b] and [b]Draw[/b] work as a pair. Throw away what you cannot use, and the draw refills you to seven.

But mind what you spend. Click your pennant to open it. The middle number is your [b]draw deck[/b].

It is finite. Nothing shuffles your discards back in. When it is empty, the Draw step gives you nothing.

And the enemy can burn it for you. Some cards make you discard straight off the top of your [b]draw deck[/b].

Once it is empty, every card you cannot discard costs you [b]one victory point[/b].

And the [b]goal[/b], General.

A full war runs at most [b]20 rounds[/b]; this lesson runs three. Have the higher team score at the end, and the war is yours. But it can end sooner.

The score is judged only at the [b]end of a round[/b], after the [b]United States[/b] has finished its turn.

If a team is [b]30 or more points ahead[/b] then, the war stops and that team has won.

The round counter here tells you how far along the war is.

Nobody will pull 30 points ahead in this lesson, so it will run all three rounds.

And [b]Germany[/b] opens, as they always do. There is nothing for you to do here but watch.

Watch what they take, General. You will have to answer it.

Germany has built an army in [b]Western Europe[/b], the coast opposite you.

That country holds a [b]supply star[/b]. It keeps their army supplied, and pays them [b]2 victory points[/b] at every Victory step they still hold it.

Turn two. The [b]United Kingdom[/b] answers, and the United Kingdom is you.

One card. Make it count.

Your [b]Play[/b] step: one card per turn.

You cannot march into Western Europe from an island. First you have to reach it. Play [b]Build Navy[/b]; the rest of your hand is greyed out for now.

steps.note: Build Army stays visible but unplayable, so the player can see what they are not doing yet.

steps.text:
The [b]North Sea[/b] touches both your home islands and Western Europe, and for the moment nobody holds it.

Select the [b]North Sea[/b] to build your navy there.

The fleet is at sea. Well done, General.

The North Sea has no supply star, so it scores nothing. What it buys is [b]position[/b].

You can only attack a country next to one of your supplied units. Your fleet now stands next to Western Europe.

Germany took points. You took the reach to take them back.

A navy needs a [b]harbour[/b]: it is built in, and stays supplied in, a sea touching a coast your team holds.

The North Sea touches the United Kingdom. Cut a fleet off from every friendly coast and the Supply step removes it.

Each faction can have only one army or navy in a country at a time.

You cannot share a country with an enemy, but you can with an ally. A country holding two units has to be battled twice to clear it.

A supply star shared with an ally pays each of you only [b]1 point[/b] instead of 2.

Each of you scores it in your own Victory step, if you are still there by then.

The [b]Victory[/b] step. You score each [b]supply star[/b] you occupy: 2 points alone, 1 shared.

The North Sea pays nothing. Your points come from the [b]United Kingdom[/b] itself.

Your [b]Discard[/b] step. Throw away anything you cannot use, or keep the lot.

Whatever you let go, the [b]Draw[/b] step fills you back up to seven.
[b]Japan[/b]. Watch this one closely, General. They are not going to build anything.

Japan spent its whole Play step laying one card [b]face down[/b]. Nothing built, nothing attacked.

That is a [b]Response[/b] card. It can never be used from the hand; it must be on the table first.

Now it waits for the [b]trigger[/b] on its face. When that happens, on anybody's turn, Japan may use it for free.

Then it is spent: flipped face up and discarded. One card, one use.

Across a real table you would see only its back, and knowing Japan holds [i]something[/i] is half its worth.

Here you hold all six seats, so you can read it.

[b]Destroyer Transport[/b]: [i]Use when you battle a sea space. Build 1 or 2 Armies adjacent to the space just battled.[/i]

Japan needs a sea battle before it is worth anything. And nobody is ever forced to use a Response.
[b]The Soviet Union[/b]. Another card to the table, and look at the difference.

The Soviets played [b]Women Conscripts[/b] [b]face up[/b]. That is a [b]Status[/b] card.

Same price as a Response: the whole Play step. Two differences, and both matter.

First, everyone can read it, so you can plan around it.

Second, it [b]stays[/b]. A Response is used once and thrown away. A Status card works every time its trigger comes round, for the rest of the war.
[b]Women Conscripts[/b]: [i]Use when you play a Build Army card for your Play step. Place that Build Army card on the top of your draw deck instead of discarding it.[/i]

So every Soviet Build Army goes back on top of their deck, to be drawn and built again.

Remember what a dry deck costs, General. The Soviets have made sure theirs lasts.
[b]Italy[/b]. A navy, and they have picked their water carefully.

Italy has taken the [b]Mediterranean Sea[/b]. No supply star, not a single point.

But it touches [b]Western Europe[/b], [b]Italy[/b], the [b]Balkans[/b], [b]North Africa[/b] and the [b]Middle East[/b].

Two of its exits are [b]straits[/b]: narrow water a land space controls.

[b]North Africa[/b] guards the way to the North Sea, the [b]Middle East[/b] the way to the Bay of Bengal. The team holding that land holds the door.

Neither of those two pays a point either, General.

Some countries are worth holding for what they [b]score[/b]. Others for what they [b]reach[/b], or deny the other side.
[b]The United States[/b], last of the six and the furthest from anything.

An army in [b]US West[/b]: a supply star worth 2 points a turn, and nothing on this board can touch it.

The Americans are rich and safe. They are also nowhere near this war.

From [b]US East[/b] to the fighting: the [b]North Atlantic[/b], the [b]North Sea[/b], then [b]Western Europe[/b]. Three plays, three turns.

Germany reached a supply star on turn one. The US cannot reach Western Europe before its fourth.

Each faction is strong somewhere and helpless elsewhere. Germany is fast and central, Japan spread across an ocean, the Americans slow, and you an island with the finest navy afloat.

Learn which is which.

Every faction has now scored. That is the end of the [b]round[/b], and the only moment the war can be won.

Nobody is 30 points ahead, so it goes on.

One full round, General: the map, the five steps, a build, a supply star, a Response, a Status card, and five rivals.

Two rounds left, and nobody will hold your hand through them.

Three rounds. Every game runs the same way: the same five steps and six factions, over twenty rounds instead of three.

Well done, General. [b]Dismissed.[/b]
